answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: trad. 6th century BC · Chinese sage, reputed author of the Tao Te Ching
answer.sourceLine: This is a genuine line from Chapter 33 of the Tao Te Ching — the classical Chinese “知人者智，自知者明” (“to know others is wisdom; to know oneself is enlightenment”). The exact English wording shown is a modern translator’s rendering: it appears verbatim in Ch’u Ta-Kao’s 1937 translation ↗ and, identically, in Wing-Tsit Chan’s 1963 translation ↗.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Attributed to Lao Tzu (Laozi); text now regarded as a compilation
Ch’u Ta-Kao (1937); identical wording in Wing-Tsit Chan (1963)

source.excerpt: He who knows others is wise; He who knows himself is enlightened. He who conquers others is strong; He who conquers himself is mighty. He who knows contentment is rich. He who keeps on his course with energy has will. He who does not deviate from his proper place will long endure. He who may die but not perish has longevity.
trail: The line is Chapter 33 of the Tao Te Ching; the classical Chinese “知人者智，自知者明” can be read on the Chinese Text Project ↗.

This precise English wording — “wise…enlightened” — appears verbatim in Ch’u Ta-Kao’s translation (first published London, The Buddhist Society, 1937) ↗ and identically in Wing-Tsit Chan’s 1963 rendering ↗.
Other standard translations word it differently — Legge (1891) has “discerning…intelligent,” D. C. Lau (1963) “clever…discernment” — as the side-by-side comparison at egreenway ↗ shows.
Whether one man named Lao Tzu wrote any of it is doubtful: modern scholarship treats his biography as later legend ↗ and the book as a compilation.
source.excerptNote: Chapter 33 in full, in Ch’u Ta-Kao’s 1937 translation. The famous couplet is the opening pair of lines.

source.rightsNote: The ancient Chinese original is public domain, but the English wording displayed here is a 20th-century translation. It was first published by Ch’u Ta-Kao in 1937 (London, The Buddhist Society) and appears identically in Wing-Tsit Chan’s 1963 version — both post-1930 and by identifiable translators, so the specific rendering is treated as in copyright in the United States. Quote the underlying idea freely; reproducing this exact English phrasing at length may implicate the translators’ rights.

author.heading: About Lao Tzu
author.metaLine: trad. 6th century BC · Chinese sage · reputed author of the Tao Te Ching
author.bio: Lao Tzu (“Old Master,” also romanized Laozi) is the semi-legendary figure traditionally credited with writing the Tao Te Ching, the foundational text of Taoism. Tradition, following Sima Qian’s Records of the Grand Historian, makes him a 6th-century-BC archivist and elder contemporary of Confucius. Modern scholarship, however, generally treats his biography as later legend and the text as a compilation of Taoist sayings assembled during the Warring States period.

misattribution.heading: Real quote, modern words
misattribution.intro: This is not a fake Lao Tzu quote — the thought is squarely Chapter 33 of the Tao Te Ching. The subtlety is that the crisp English one-liner people share is one translator’s choice of words, not an ancient phrase, and it is often passed around with no sense that a 20th-century hand shaped it.

items.why: “Wise…enlightened” is a specific rendering. It appears verbatim in Ch’u Ta-Kao (1937) ↗ and Wing-Tsit Chan (1963) ↗, but other standard versions say “discerning,” “clever,” or “intelligent” instead — see the translation comparison ↗.

items.who: “Lao Tzu” as a single historical man
items.why: Crediting the line to one sage is convention, not established fact: modern scholarship regards Laozi’s biography as later invention ↗ and the Tao Te Ching as a compilation by many hands.

misattribution.truthLine: Verdict: a real line from Tao Te Ching ch. 33 ↗, faithfully translated — just remember the memorable English is a modern translator’s, and “Lao Tzu” is a traditional byline.

context.heading: Why it endures
lead: Chapter 33 sets up a ladder of paradoxes: knowing others versus knowing oneself, conquering others versus conquering oneself. The couplet works because it quietly demotes the achievement the world prizes — understanding and mastering other people — beneath the harder, inward work of self-knowledge.

The line travels well partly because two of its most-reprinted English versions, Ch’u Ta-Kao’s and Wing-Tsit Chan’s, happen to word it identically and memorably, giving the internet a single clean sentence to circulate.
